passage: The reference desk existed to answer the one question a catalogue could not: what the library had that a reader would not have thought to ask for. Its decline is usually described as a fall in demand, and the description is defensible only if the demand is for a person. In 1994 the reference desk at one mid-sized library logged nine thousand questions. Ten years later it logged twelve hundred, and the reading rooms had not emptied. What had changed was the arrival of a body of information that was exhaustive, current, and available without anyone in the building. The reference librarian was not answering a question the catalogue had failed to answer. She was answering a question the catalogue could now answer better, faster, and without knowing which of the two the reader actually wanted. The profession spent the following decade arguing about retrieval, and the argument was beside the point. The desk had not been a search function. It had been a judgement function: a person deciding what was worth asking, and often, having read the question aloud to the room, discovering that the person who had come in with a question did not have it. That cannot be catalogued and has never been available on demand. It is also the only part of the answer that was ever about the reader rather than the book.

passage: The group's first recording was made in 1917 and it is not a tune.
